title: Introduce workload-sliced performance profiles and autogen release clauses
author: Marina Cheng
description:
Motivation: Users have asked for finer-grained model profiles that capture cost/latency behavior across realistic workload slices (short vs. long context, batch vs. single-request, embedding vs. decode-heavy). This PR adds a workload-slicing step to onboarding that produces multiple perf profiles per model and an automated release-clause generator that synthesizes human-readable release notes focused on which workload slices changed materially. The generator emits short clauses suitable for the model registry CHANGELOG and for inclusion in rollout notifications.

What this changes: 1) onboarding pipeline: a new 'slice-prober' stage that runs a compact set of micro-benchmarks across predefined workload slices and emits per-slice metrics and stability flags; 2) profile format: extend profile manifest with a top-level "slices" array (name, sample-seed, latency_p50/90, cost_token_estimate, stability_score); 3) changelog helper: heuristic-based clause synthesizer that compares previous and current slice metrics and drafts concise release clauses (e.g., "Improved vdecode throughput on long-context slices, ~12% p90 latency reduction"); 4) provenance: attach stable fingerprint and run metadata (kernel hints, quantization profile) to each slice entry for reproducibility.

Checklist: - [x] slice-prober implementation + unit tests - [x] profile manifest schema bump (+ migration op for existing manifests) - [x] release-clause synthesizer + golden examples - [x] CLI flag to opt-out of auto-drafts (--no-autodraft) - [x] small UX addition: sample slice view in model readme generator - [x] docs stub in onboarding guide

Related: ENG-8421 (workload-sliced profiles), ENG-8468 (changelog automation), SUP-4120 (customer-reported variance on long-context workloads).

review_conversation:
Ayesha: Could you clarify how slice sample seeds are chosen and whether they are stable across runs?
Author (Marina): Seeds are deterministic by default (model_id + version + slice-name) to keep probes reproducible; there's a flag to add jitter for noisy workloads.
Liam: The migration script concerns me for very large registries — can we run the migration lazily?
Author: Migration is implemented as a background backfill job (onboard/migrations/0003_add_slices.py) that annotates manifests on first read; the PR contains a safe fast-path for users who prefer an offline backfill.
Diego: The heuristics sometimes mark tiny improvements as noteworthy; can we add a significance floor?
Author: Added a stability_score threshold and a configurable significance floor (default 3% relative for p90) — included in tests.
Ayesha: CI flake on macOS runner unrelated to this change; re-run passed.
Liam: approve after comments addressed.
Diego: approved.
Merge bot: squash-merged by Marina on 2026-02-23.
ci_checks_summary: CI: unit (pass), integration (pass), lint (pass), mypy (pass), benchmark-smoke (pass). One transient macOS flake was retried and passed.
release_notes:
- Add workload-sliced performance profiles (manifest v2) that capture per-slice latency and cost estimates.
- Autogenerated release clauses that highlight which workload slices changed materially between versions (opt-out via --no-autodraft).
- Backwards-compatible manifest migration (lazy backfill).
notes_for_ops: Backfill strategy: registry operators can trigger the offline backfill with bin/redwood-model-registry migrate-slices --batch-size=500. Default runtime uses lazy annotation on first manifest read; storage impact is ~120 bytes per added slice. Monitor provenance index growth after rollout.
examples_and_golden_outputs: docs/onboarding/slices.md contains golden release-clause examples and explanation of stability_score
qa_notes: Manual QA: - run onboarding against small model (toy) with default slices and verify manifest v2; - run onboard with --no-autodraft and verify no draft clause appears; - run backfill on a snapshot registry and ensure manifests are annotated without downtime.
security_considerations: No new secrets. Probes run in a sandboxed harness and have a request budget to avoid accidental usage spikes. Autodraft text is sanitized before insertion into registry notes to avoid injection in downstream UIs.
